topic: Test process, testware, roles and skills

notes.front: What is a test process?
notes.back: A set of test activities performed to achieve a test objective.
notes.explanation: The syllabus adds that which activities it holds, how they are done and when, is normally decided during test planning.
notes.example: Like the steps of a recipe, picked to produce one particular dish.
notes.evidence: A set of test activities performed to achieve a test objective.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test process”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is test planning?
notes.back: The activity of establishing or updating a test plan.
notes.explanation: In the syllabus, planning defines the test objectives and then selects an approach that best achieves them within the constraints of the context.
notes.example: Like planning a road trip: first where you want to end up, then the route that fits your time and money.
notes.evidence: The activity of establishing or updating a test plan.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test planning”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is test monitoring?
notes.back: The activity that checks the status of testing activities, identifies variances from what was planned or expected, and reports status to stakeholders.
notes.explanation: In the syllabus it runs throughout testing: every test activity is checked and actual progress is measured against the plan.
notes.example: Like a sat-nav telling you that you are now 20 minutes behind your planned arrival time.
notes.evidence: The activity that checks the status of testing activities, identifies any variances from planned or expected, and reports status to stakeholders.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test monitoring”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is test control?
notes.back: The activity that develops and applies corrective actions to get a test project back on track when it deviates from the plan.
notes.explanation: Monitoring spots the deviation; control acts on it, taking the actions needed to meet the test objectives.
notes.example: Like the driver switching to a faster road once the sat-nav reports the delay.
notes.evidence: The activity that develops and applies corrective actions to get a test project on track when it deviates from what was planned.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test control”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is test analysis?
notes.back: The activity that identifies test conditions by analysing the test basis.
notes.explanation: In the syllabus, test analysis answers the question “what to test?”.
notes.example: Like reading a new board game’s rulebook to list which rules need trying out, before deciding how to try each one.
notes.evidence: The activity that identifies test conditions by analyzing the test basis.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test analysis”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is the test basis?
notes.back: The body of knowledge used as the basis for test analysis and test design.
notes.explanation: Test analysis examines it to find what to test, and also evaluates it for defects and testability.
notes.example: Like the rulebook in the board-game example: the source that decides what counts as right.
notes.evidence: The body of knowledge used as the basis for test analysis and test design.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test basis”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a test condition?
notes.back: A testable aspect of a component or system that is intended to be tested.
notes.explanation: Test analysis defines test conditions and prioritises them, taking the related risks into account.
notes.example: For a hotel booking site: “a booking can be cancelled free of charge up to 48 hours before arrival”.
notes.evidence: A testable aspect of a component or system that is intended to be tested.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test condition”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is test design?
notes.back: The activity that derives and specifies test cases from test conditions.
notes.explanation: In the syllabus, test design answers the question “how to test?”.
notes.example: Like turning a list of revision topics into specific practice questions with model answers.
notes.evidence: The activity that derives and specifies test cases from test conditions.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test design”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a test case?
notes.back: A set of preconditions, inputs, actions (where applicable), expected results and postconditions, developed from test conditions.
notes.explanation: The expected results are what test execution later compares the actual results with.
notes.example: Precondition: a hotel booking exists for arrival in 3 days. Action: cancel it. Expected result: a full refund is shown.
notes.evidence: A set of preconditions, inputs, actions (where applicable), expected results and postconditions, developed based on test conditions.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test case”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is test data?
notes.back: Data needed for test execution.
notes.explanation: The syllabus puts defining test data requirements in test design, and creating or acquiring the data in test implementation.
notes.example: Like the guest profiles and bookings that must already exist before the cancellation test can be run.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test data”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is test implementation?
notes.back: The activity that prepares the testware needed for test execution.
notes.explanation: It includes creating or acquiring test data, organising test cases into procedures and scripts, and setting up the test environment.
notes.example: Like laying out the ingredients and heating the oven before any cooking starts.
notes.evidence: The activity that prepares the testware needed for test execution.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test implementation”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a test procedure?
notes.back: A sequence of test cases in execution order, with any actions needed to set up preconditions beforehand and wrap up afterwards.
notes.explanation: Test implementation organises test cases into test procedures.
notes.example: Log in as a booking agent, create a booking, cancel it, check the refund, then delete the test booking.
notes.evidence: A sequence of test cases in execution order and any associated actions that may be required to set up the initial preconditions and any wrap-up activities after execution.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test procedure”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a test suite?
notes.back: A set of test procedures grouped together, as test implementation often does.
notes.explanation: Assembling suites is part of test implementation, after test cases have been organised into procedures.
notes.example: Like a playlist: every procedure for the booking area bundled together for the nightly run.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a test execution schedule?
notes.back: The arrangement of prioritised test procedures that sets their order for efficient test execution.
notes.explanation: It is prepared in test implementation, and test execution then runs the tests in accordance with it.
notes.example: Like a sports day timetable that sets which events run in which order so the day flows.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is test execution?
notes.back: The activity that runs a test on a component or system, producing actual results.
notes.explanation: The actual results it produces are then compared with the expected results.
notes.example: Like actually sitting a practice paper, rather than preparing it.
notes.evidence: The activity that runs a test on a component or system producing actual results.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test execution”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a test result?
notes.back: The status of the execution of a test.
notes.explanation: The glossary also lists outcome and test outcome as synonyms; the syllabus says results are logged during test execution.
notes.example: Like the tick or cross marked against each question of a practice paper.
notes.evidence: The status of the execution of a test.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test result”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is test completion?
notes.back: The activity that makes testware available for later use, leaves test environments in a satisfactory condition and reports testing results to stakeholders.
notes.explanation: In the syllabus it usually happens at project milestones, such as a release or the end of an iteration.
notes.example: Like tidying up after a dinner party: storing the leftovers, cleaning the kitchen and telling the host how it went.
notes.evidence: The activity that makes testware available for later use, leaves test environments in a satisfactory condition and communicates the results of testing to relevant stakeholders.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test completion”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is testware?
notes.back: Work products produced during the test process for use in planning, designing, executing, evaluating and reporting on testing.
notes.explanation: Each test activity produces its own testware, and the syllabus says its list of examples is not exhaustive.
notes.example: Like everything a film crew produces besides the film itself: scripts, shot lists, call sheets and continuity notes.
notes.evidence: Work products produced during the test process for use in planning, designing, executing, evaluating and reporting on testing.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “testware”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a risk register?
notes.back: A list of risks, each with its likelihood, its impact and information about how it is mitigated.
notes.explanation: It is a test planning work product and is often part of the test plan.
notes.example: Like a ship’s list of hazards for a voyage, each with how likely and how bad it is and what the crew will do about it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is traceability?
notes.back: The ability to establish explicit relationships between related work products or items within work products.
notes.explanation: In testing, the syllabus applies it between test basis elements, their testware, test results and defects.
notes.example: Like a parcel’s tracking number, which links the order, the warehouse slip and the delivery receipt.
notes.evidence: The ability to establish explicit relationships between related work products or items within work products.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “traceability”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is the test management role?
notes.back: The role with overall responsibility for the test process, the test team and the leadership of test activities.
notes.explanation: It is mainly focused on test planning, monitoring, control and completion.
notes.example: Like a film’s producer, who owns the schedule and the crew rather than operating the camera.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the testing role?
notes.back: The role with overall responsibility for the engineering, or technical, side of testing.
notes.explanation: It is mainly focused on test analysis, test design, test implementation and test execution.
notes.example: Like the camera and sound crew, who do the technical work that produces the film.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the whole team approach?
notes.back: A way of working in which anyone with the right skills may take on any task, and the whole team answers for quality.
notes.explanation: It builds on a tester’s ability to work well in a team and contribute to the team’s goals.
notes.example: Like a small restaurant where cooks, waiters and the owner all pitch in wherever needed and all answer for the food.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is independence of testing?
notes.back: The degree to which a work product is tested by people other than its author.
notes.explanation: The syllabus grades it from none, when the author tests, to very high, when testers come from outside the organisation.
notes.example: Like the difference between proofreading your own essay and having a stranger proofread it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Testing depends on context, so why does the syllabus still describe common sets of test activities?
notes.back: Without them, testing is less likely to achieve its test objectives.
notes.explanation: Taken together, these common sets of activities make up a test process.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4 “Test Activities, Testware and Test Roles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When is it normally decided which test activities the test process includes, how they are done and when?
notes.back: During test planning for the specific situation.
notes.explanation: The test process can be tailored to a situation based on various factors.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4 “Test Activities, Testware and Test Roles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A new team asks whether it must copy, activity for activity, the test process its previous project used. What does the syllabus suggest?
notes.back: No: the test process is tailored to the situation, normally during test planning.
notes.explanation: Which activities are included, and how and when they happen, depend on the specific situation.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4 “Test Activities, Testware and Test Roles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Are the main groups of test activities always carried out one after another?
notes.back: No. They may look like a logical sequence, but they are often done iteratively or in parallel.
notes.explanation: They also usually need tailoring to the system and the project.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a two-week iteration, a tester designs tests for one story while running the tests for another. Is that a departure from the test process?
notes.back: No: test activities are often carried out in parallel or iteratively.
notes.explanation: The groups of activities only appear sequential; in practice they overlap.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How many main groups of test activities does the syllabus describe?
notes.back: Seven.
notes.explanation: The syllabus gives no number, but it describes seven: planning; monitoring and control, treated together; analysis; design; implementation; execution; completion.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which group of test activities defines the test objectives and chooses an approach to meet them?
notes.back: Test planning.
notes.explanation: Planning sets the objectives and approach that the rest of the process works to.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which group of test activities compares progress with the plan and takes action to meet the objectives?
notes.back: Test monitoring and test control.
notes.explanation: Monitoring checks progress against the plan; control takes the actions needed to meet the objectives.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity answers the question “what to test?”
notes.back: Test analysis.
notes.explanation: It works from the test basis and expresses its answer in measurable coverage criteria.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity answers the question “how to test?”
notes.back: Test design.
notes.explanation: It turns the test conditions from analysis into test cases and other testware.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity creates or acquires the testware needed for test execution?
notes.back: Test implementation.
notes.explanation: It covers everything from test data to the test environment, before any test is run.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity runs the tests in line with the test execution schedule?
notes.back: Test execution.
notes.explanation: Each such run is called a test run.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity usually takes place at project milestones?
notes.back: Test completion.
notes.explanation: Milestones include a release, the end of an iteration and the completion of a test level.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Test planning first sets the test objectives, then picks the approach that meets them best within the {{c1::constraints}} of the wider context.
notes.explanation: Planning first defines the objectives; the approach is then chosen to fit what the context allows.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the syllabus, what does test monitoring involve?
notes.back: Continually checking every test activity and measuring actual progress against the plan.
notes.explanation: It supplies the information that test control then acts on.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the syllabus, what does test control involve?
notes.back: Doing whatever is needed so that the test objectives are still met.
notes.explanation: Where monitoring shows a deviation from the plan, control is the response.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does test monitoring differ from test control?
notes.back: Monitoring checks progress against the plan; control takes the actions needed to meet the test objectives.
notes.explanation: One observes and reports, the other intervenes.
notes.contrast: Monitoring: where are we against the plan? Control: what do we do about it?
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Halfway through testing, the test lead sees only 40% of the planned tests have run and moves two testers from a finished area to the lagging one. Which part is monitoring and which is control?
notes.back: Spotting the 40% is test monitoring; moving the testers is test control.
notes.explanation: Comparing progress with the plan is monitoring; acting to get back on track is control.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before a project starts, the test lead decides that the aim is to show the new tariff rules work and picks risk-based testing within a four-week window. Which test activity is this?
notes.back: Test planning.
notes.explanation: Defining the objectives and choosing an approach within the constraints is what planning consists of.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In test analysis, what is analysed, and to identify what?
notes.back: The test basis, to identify testable features.
notes.explanation: Test conditions associated with those features are then defined and prioritised.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How are test conditions handled during test analysis?
notes.back: They are defined and prioritised, taking the related risks and risk levels into account.
notes.explanation: Risk-based testing, which uses these risk levels, is covered in chapter 5.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides finding test conditions, what does test analysis evaluate the test basis and the test object for?
notes.back: Defects they may contain, and their testability.
notes.explanation: Defects found in the test basis are reported as analysis work products when they are not fixed straight away.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In what terms does test analysis answer “what to test?”?
notes.back: In terms of measurable coverage criteria.
notes.explanation: Traceability later uses such criteria to evaluate coverage.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Testers often use {{c1::test techniques}} to help them with test analysis.
notes.explanation: The same techniques, covered in chapter 4 of the syllabus, also support test design.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester reads the user stories for a loan application form and notes “an applicant under 18 is refused” as something to test. Which test activity is this?
notes.back: Test analysis: identifying a test condition from the test basis.
notes.explanation: Deciding what to test from the stories is analysis; deciding exactly how comes next, in design.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: While analysing a refund requirement, a tester sees it says “within 3 days” in one place and “within 5 days” in another. Is flagging this part of test analysis?
notes.back: Yes. Test analysis also evaluates the test basis for defects.
notes.explanation: The contradiction is a defect in the test basis, found without running anything.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does test design elaborate the test conditions into?
notes.back: Test cases and other testware, such as test charters.
notes.explanation: Test design turns test conditions from analysis into something that can be run.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In test design, what role do coverage items play?
notes.back: They serve as a guide for specifying test case inputs.
notes.explanation: Identifying coverage items is often part of test design, and test techniques can support it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides test cases, what does test design define, design or identify?
notes.back: Test data requirements, the design of the test environment, and the infrastructure and tools needed.
notes.explanation: Test implementation later creates or acquires what design specified.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does test analysis differ from test design?
notes.back: Analysis answers “what to test?”; design answers “how to test?”.
notes.explanation: Analysis yields test conditions; design turns them into test cases.
notes.contrast: What to test (conditions) versus how to test (cases).
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The tester turns “an applicant under 18 is refused” into a case: date of birth making the applicant 17 years and 364 days old, with the refusal message expected. Which test activity is this?
notes.back: Test design.
notes.explanation: It derives a test case, with inputs and an expected result, from a test condition.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which of these tasks belongs to test design rather than test analysis?
notes.back: B: designing the test environment.
notes.choices:
A) Prioritising test conditions by risk
B) Designing the test environment
C) Evaluating the testability of the test basis
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are both tasks of test analysis, which works on the test basis and the test conditions.
notes.explanation: Test design includes designing the test environment and identifying infrastructure and tools.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How are test cases organised during test implementation?
notes.back: Into test procedures, which are often assembled into test suites.
notes.explanation: Organising and assembling them is a step between design and execution.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which kinds of test scripts are created in test implementation?
notes.back: Both manual and automated test scripts.
notes.explanation: The v4.0.1 errata changed “automated test scripts” to “manual and automated test scripts” in the testware list.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19; Appendix C “Release Notes”, p. 73
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is done with test procedures to prepare for efficient test execution?
notes.back: They are prioritised and arranged within a test execution schedule.
notes.explanation: The schedule then governs the order in which tests are run.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What happens to the test environment during test implementation?
notes.back: It is built and verified to be set up correctly.
notes.explanation: Test design only designed the environment; implementation builds it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester loads 200 fictional customer accounts into the staging database and writes the script that logs in as each one. Which test activity is this?
notes.back: Test implementation.
notes.explanation: Creating test data and scripts ready for execution is implementation, not execution itself.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides a plain manual or automated run, what are two forms test execution can take?
notes.back: Continuous testing and pair testing sessions.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says test execution can take many forms, so the list is open.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: During test execution, what is compared with what?
notes.back: Actual test results with expected results.
notes.explanation: The expected results come from the test cases written in test design.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: During test execution, the test results are {{c1::logged}}.
notes.explanation: Test logs are a work product of test execution.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why are anomalies analysed during test execution?
notes.back: To find what probably caused each one, so it can be reported in terms of the failures actually seen.
notes.explanation: The analysis comes before reporting, so reports rest on the failures actually observed.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester runs tonight’s scheduled procedures, sees the refund screen show £0 where £40 was expected, and records it. Which test activity is this?
notes.back: Test execution.
notes.explanation: Running tests, comparing actual with expected results and logging them are all execution tasks.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: At what kind of point does test completion usually take place?
notes.back: At project milestones, such as a release, the end of an iteration or the completion of a test level.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names release, end of iteration and test level completion as examples.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In test completion, what is created for defects that are still unresolved?
notes.back: Change requests or product backlog items.
notes.explanation: Unresolved defects are handed on, not dropped.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In test completion, what happens to testware that may be useful in future?
notes.back: It is identified and archived, or handed over to the appropriate teams.
notes.explanation: Testware that may be useful later is kept or passed on rather than lost.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In test completion, what happens to the test environment?
notes.back: It is shut down to an agreed state.
notes.explanation: Shutting it down to an agreed state, rather than just abandoning it, is how completion leaves test environments in a satisfactory condition.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In test completion, what is analysed to learn for the future?
notes.back: The test activities, to find lessons learned and improvements for future iterations, releases or projects.
notes.explanation: The syllabus points to section 2.1.6, on retrospectives, for this task.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What report does test completion produce, and who receives it?
notes.back: A test completion report, communicated to the stakeholders.
notes.explanation: Reporting results to stakeholders is part of the glossary’s own definition of test completion.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: At the end of a release, four minor defects are still open. What does test completion do about them?
notes.back: B: creates change requests or product backlog items.
notes.choices:
A) Leaves them in the test log only
B) Creates change requests or product backlog items for them
C) Delays completion until all are fixed
notes.choicesExplained: A would lose track of them. C is not what the syllabus describes: unresolved defects are handed on, not a bar to completion.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says change requests or backlog items are created for unresolved defects.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After a release, the team stores its regression scripts in the shared repository, resets the staging servers as agreed and holds a lessons-learned session. Which test activity is this?
notes.back: Test completion.
notes.explanation: Archiving testware, returning the environment to an agreed state and learning lessons are all completion tasks.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.1 “Test Activities and Tasks”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does the way testing is carried out depend on context?
notes.back: Testing is part of the organisation’s development processes, is funded by stakeholders, and aims to help meet their business needs.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says testing is not performed in isolation.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which contextual factor covers needs, expectations, requirements and willingness to cooperate?
notes.back: Stakeholders.
notes.explanation: It is one of eight contextual factors the syllabus lists, and the lists in brackets are open-ended.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which contextual factor covers skills, knowledge, level of experience, availability and training needs?
notes.back: Team members.
notes.explanation: It is one of eight contextual factors the syllabus lists, and the lists in brackets are open-ended.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which contextual factor covers the test object’s criticality, identified risks, market needs and specific legal regulations?
notes.back: The business domain.
notes.explanation: It is one of eight contextual factors the syllabus lists, and the lists in brackets are open-ended.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which contextual factor covers the type of software, the product architecture and the technology used?
notes.back: Technical factors.
notes.explanation: It is one of eight contextual factors the syllabus lists, and the lists in brackets are open-ended.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which contextual factor covers scope, time, budget and resources?
notes.back: Project constraints.
notes.explanation: It is one of eight contextual factors the syllabus lists, and the lists in brackets are open-ended.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which contextual factor covers organisational structure, existing policies and the practices used?
notes.back: Organisational factors.
notes.explanation: It is one of eight contextual factors the syllabus lists, and the lists in brackets are open-ended.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which contextual factor covers engineering practices and development methods?
notes.back: The software development lifecycle.
notes.explanation: It is one of eight contextual factors the syllabus lists, and the lists in brackets are open-ended.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which contextual factor covers the availability, usability and compliance of tools?
notes.back: Tools.
notes.explanation: It is one of eight contextual factors the syllabus lists, and the lists in brackets are open-ended.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team testing software for heart monitors must satisfy strict medical-device rules. Which contextual factor is this mainly?
notes.back: A: the business domain.
notes.choices:
A) Business domain
B) Tools
C) Team members
notes.choicesExplained: B concerns tool availability, usability and compliance. C concerns people’s skills and availability.
notes.explanation: Criticality of the test object and specific legal regulations both fall under the business domain.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Half the testers on a project are new graduates who have never written an automated test. Which contextual factor does this describe?
notes.back: B: team members.
notes.choices:
A) Project constraints
B) Team members
C) Stakeholders
notes.choicesExplained: A concerns scope, time, budget and resources. C concerns the needs and cooperation of those with a stake.
notes.explanation: Skills, experience and training needs are all listed under team members.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The launch date is fixed by a trade fair and cannot move, and the testing budget was cut by a third. Which contextual factor is at work?
notes.back: A: project constraints.
notes.choices:
A) Project constraints
B) Organisational factors
C) Technical factors
notes.choicesExplained: B concerns structure, policies and practices. C concerns the software, its architecture and technology.
notes.explanation: Time and budget are both project constraints.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 19
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two test-related issues that contextual factors affect?
notes.back: For example, the test strategy and the degree of test automation.
notes.explanation: The syllabus’s list is open; it also includes test techniques, required coverage, level of detail of testware and test reporting.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A regulated bank keeps very detailed testware, while a two-person start-up keeps its testware light. What explains the difference?
notes.back: Context: contextual factors affect issues such as the level of detail of testware.
notes.explanation: Regulation and team size are contextual factors, and the level of detail of testware is among the issues they influence.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.2 “Test Process in Context”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is the syllabus’s list of testware complete?
notes.back: No. It is not exhaustive, and organisations vary a lot in how they produce, name, organise and manage work products.
notes.explanation: Each organisation shapes its testware in its own way.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What ensures the consistency and integrity of testware and other work products?
notes.back: Proper configuration management.
notes.explanation: The syllabus covers configuration management in chapter 5.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity produces the test plan and the entry and exit criteria?
notes.back: Test planning.
notes.explanation: The test schedule, risk register, entry and exit criteria are often part of the test plan.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity produces the risk register and the test schedule?
notes.back: Test planning.
notes.explanation: Both are planning work products, and both are often part of the test plan.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity produces test progress reports and documented control directives?
notes.back: Test monitoring and test control.
notes.explanation: Progress reports record what monitoring found; control directives record the actions control took.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides progress reports and control directives, what else do test monitoring and test control produce?
notes.back: Information about risks.
notes.explanation: Information about risks appears among the work products of monitoring and control.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity produces prioritised test conditions, such as acceptance criteria?
notes.back: Test analysis.
notes.explanation: Conditions are the main output of analysis: its answer to “what to test?”.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which defect reports come out of test analysis?
notes.back: Reports on defects in the test basis, where these are not fixed directly.
notes.explanation: Test analysis evaluates the test basis for defects.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity produces test charters and coverage items?
notes.back: Test design.
notes.explanation: Design elaborates conditions into test cases and other testware, test charters included.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity produces test data requirements and test environment requirements?
notes.back: Test design.
notes.explanation: Design states what will be needed; implementation later provides it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity produces test procedures, test suites and the test execution schedule?
notes.back: Test implementation.
notes.explanation: These are the outputs of organising and ordering test cases for execution.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity produces the test data itself and the test environment items?
notes.back: Test implementation.
notes.explanation: Implementation creates or acquires what design only specified.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity produces test logs?
notes.back: Test execution.
notes.explanation: Logging test results is a task of execution.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity produces action items for improvement and documented lessons learned?
notes.back: Test completion.
notes.explanation: Completion analyses the test activities to improve later projects or iterations.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activity’s work products include change requests, for example as product backlog items?
notes.back: Test completion.
notes.explanation: Unresolved defects at completion become change requests or backlog items.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Defect reports appear in the testware of two test activities. Which two?
notes.back: Test analysis (defects in the test basis) and test execution.
notes.explanation: Analysis finds defects by examining the test basis; execution finds them by running tests.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which activities produce test data requirements and test data?
notes.back: Test data requirements come from test design; the test data itself from test implementation.
notes.explanation: Design says what is needed; implementation creates or acquires it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two examples of test environment items?
notes.back: Stubs and drivers; simulators and service virtualisations are also listed.
notes.explanation: They are test implementation work products, alongside test data and test scripts.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A spreadsheet lists “key supplier goes bust: likelihood low, impact high, mitigation second supplier”, among other entries. Which work product is it, and from which activity?
notes.back: A risk register, from test planning.
notes.explanation: A list of risks with likelihood, impact and mitigation is a risk register, a planning work product.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Every Friday the project board receives one page on how many tests ran, passed, failed and are blocked against plan. Which activity produces it?
notes.back: Test monitoring and test control: it is a test progress report.
notes.explanation: Test progress reports are a work product of monitoring and control.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: From a user story, a tester writes “a user can reset a forgotten password through an emailed link”. Which activity produces this work product?
notes.back: Test analysis: it is a test condition, here in the form of an acceptance criterion.
notes.explanation: Acceptance criteria are an example of test conditions, the output of analysis.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A note reads: “Explore the checkout for 60 minutes, looking for rounding errors in discounts.” Which activity produces this work product?
notes.back: Test design: it is a test charter.
notes.explanation: Test charters are among the testware that design elaborates from test conditions.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The team builds a fake payment gateway that always answers “approved”, so checkout tests can run without the real bank. Which activity produces it?
notes.back: Test implementation: it is a test environment item.
notes.explanation: Test environment items such as simulators and stubs are implementation work products.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A file records which tests ran at 02:00, on which build, and with what results. Which activity produces it?
notes.back: Test execution: it is a test log.
notes.explanation: Logging results as tests run is part of execution.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A backlog item reads “Fix slow search results, deferred from release 3”. Which activity typically produces it?
notes.back: Test completion: it is a change request for an unresolved defect.
notes.explanation: At completion, unresolved defects are turned into change requests or backlog items.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.3 “Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For effective test monitoring and control, between what should traceability be kept throughout the test process?
notes.back: Test basis elements, the testware associated with them, test results and defects.
notes.explanation: Effective test monitoring and test control depend on it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of evaluation does accurate traceability support?
notes.back: Coverage evaluation.
notes.explanation: That is why it pays to define measurable coverage criteria in the test basis: they can serve as key performance indicators for how far the test objectives are met.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 20
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can tracing test cases to requirements verify?
notes.back: That the requirements are covered by test cases.
notes.explanation: It is one of the syllabus’s examples of traceability supporting coverage evaluation.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can tracing test results to risks be used to evaluate?
notes.back: The level of residual risk in the test object.
notes.explanation: It is the syllabus’s second example of traceability supporting coverage evaluation.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An auditor asks whether every requirement in a car-insurance quote specification has at least one test. What makes this question answerable?
notes.back: Traceability from test cases to requirements.
notes.explanation: Links from test cases to requirements show which requirements have tests.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before release, the manager asks how much risk remains in the payments module given the latest test results. Which traceability answers this?
notes.back: Traceability of test results to risks.
notes.explanation: Linking results to risks is what lets residual risk be evaluated.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of good traceability helps when a requirement changes?
notes.back: It makes it possible to determine the impact of the change.
notes.explanation: These benefits come on top of coverage evaluation; the syllabus lists them for good traceability.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of good traceability matters when an external inspector examines the project?
notes.back: It facilitates audits.
notes.explanation: These benefits come on top of coverage evaluation; the syllabus lists them for good traceability.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of good traceability concerns governance of information technology?
notes.back: It helps meet governance criteria for information technology.
notes.explanation: These benefits come on top of coverage evaluation; the syllabus lists them for good traceability.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does good traceability make test progress and completion reports easier to understand?
notes.back: By including the status of test basis elements.
notes.explanation: These benefits come on top of coverage evaluation; the syllabus lists them for good traceability.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Traceability provides information to assess which three things?
notes.back: Product quality, process capability, and project progress against business goals.
notes.explanation: These benefits come on top of coverage evaluation; the syllabus lists them for good traceability.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How can traceability help when talking to non-technical stakeholders?
notes.back: It can help communicate the technical aspects of testing in an understandable way.
notes.explanation: Reports that include the status of test basis elements are easier for stakeholders to follow.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The rules for loyalty points change, and the tester must find every test affected. What makes this quick?
notes.back: Traceability, which makes it possible to determine the impact of changes.
notes.explanation: Traceability links the changed requirement to its testware.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.4 “Traceability between the Test Basis and Testware”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which two principal roles in testing does the syllabus cover?
notes.back: A test management role and a testing role.
notes.explanation: They are roles, not job titles: the syllabus lets different people take them, or one person take both.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What do the activities and tasks assigned to the two roles depend on?
notes.back: Factors such as the project and product context, the skills of the people in the roles, and the organisation.
notes.explanation: The split between the two roles varies from one situation to another.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activities is the test management role mainly focused on?
notes.back: Test planning, test monitoring, test control and test completion.
notes.explanation: The role takes overall responsibility for the test process, the test team and leadership.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test activities is the testing role mainly focused on?
notes.back: Test analysis, test design, test implementation and test execution.
notes.explanation: The role takes overall responsibility for the engineering side of testing.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the test management role differ from the testing role?
notes.back: Test management owns the test process, team and leadership; the testing role owns the engineering side of testing.
notes.explanation: One leads and steers testing; the other does the technical work.
notes.contrast: Management: planning, monitoring, control, completion. Testing: analysis, design, implementation, execution.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Agile software development, who may handle some of the test management tasks?
notes.back: The Agile team.
notes.explanation: The way the test management role is carried out varies with the context.

notes.front: Who may perform test management tasks that span several teams or the whole organisation?
notes.back: Test managers outside the development team.
notes.explanation: The way the test management role is carried out varies with the context.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who can take on the test management role?
notes.back: Different people at different times, for example a team leader, a test manager or a development manager.
notes.explanation: The role is described by its responsibilities, which different people may carry.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can one person hold the testing role and the test management role?
notes.back: Yes, even at the same time.
notes.explanation: The syllabus explicitly allows this.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Setting the test objectives for the next release: which role is this task mainly for?
notes.back: The test management role (test planning).
notes.explanation: Test planning is one of the activities the test management role mainly focuses on.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Writing test cases for a new fare calculator: which role is this task mainly for?
notes.back: The testing role (test design).
notes.explanation: Test design is one of the engineering activities of the testing role.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Writing and presenting the test completion report: which role is this task mainly for?
notes.back: The test management role (test completion).
notes.explanation: Test completion falls to the test management role.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Building the test environment and checking it is set up correctly: which role is this task mainly for?
notes.back: The testing role (test implementation).
notes.explanation: Test implementation belongs to the testing role.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.4.5 “Roles in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a five-person start-up, the lead developer plans and tracks the testing, and also writes and runs tests. Is that consistent with the syllabus?
notes.back: Yes. One person can take on both the test management role and the testing role, even at the same time.
notes.explanation: The roles describe responsibilities, which may be combined in one person.

notes.front: How does the syllabus describe a skill?
notes.back: The ability to do something well, coming from one’s knowledge, practice and aptitude.
notes.explanation: Good testers need essential skills of this kind, including working in teams and at different levels of independence.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5 “Essential Skills and Good Practices in Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which generic skill increases the effectiveness of testing, for example through test techniques?
notes.back: Testing knowledge.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says these skills are generic, but particularly relevant for testers.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which generic skills help testers find defects, especially the hard-to-find ones?
notes.back: Thoroughness, carefulness, curiosity, attention to detail and being methodical.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says these skills are generic, but particularly relevant for testers.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which generic skills help testers interact with stakeholders and report and discuss defects?
notes.back: Good communication, active listening and being a team player.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says these skills are generic, but particularly relevant for testers.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which generic skills does the syllabus group with creativity, to increase the effectiveness of testing?
notes.back: Analytical thinking and critical thinking.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says these skills are generic, but particularly relevant for testers.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which generic skill increases the efficiency of testing, for example by using suitable test tools?
notes.back: Technical knowledge.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says these skills are generic, but particularly relevant for testers.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which generic skill lets testers understand and communicate with end users and business representatives?
notes.back: Domain knowledge.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says these skills are generic, but particularly relevant for testers.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does testing knowledge improve, and what does technical knowledge improve?
notes.back: Testing knowledge improves effectiveness (e.g. test techniques); technical knowledge improves efficiency (e.g. test tools).
notes.explanation: The syllabus pairs each skill with what it improves.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester joining a pensions firm spends her first weeks learning how contributions and tax relief work. Which generic skill is she building?
notes.back: Domain knowledge.
notes.explanation: It lets her understand and communicate with the business representatives and end users.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester finds a rare defect by checking every rounding step on a 30-page statement, one line at a time. Which generic skills is she showing?
notes.back: Thoroughness and attention to detail.
notes.explanation: These skills help identify defects, especially the ones that are difficult to find.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why are communication skills crucial for testers?
notes.back: Testers often bring unwelcome news, and people tend to blame whoever delivers it.
notes.explanation: Testers therefore need to be able to communicate well, especially when reporting defects.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How might the people who receive test results perceive them?
notes.back: As criticism of the product and of its author.
notes.explanation: The syllabus asks testers to communicate information about defects and failures constructively.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which bias can make it hard to accept information that disagrees with what people already believe?
notes.back: Confirmation bias.
notes.explanation: It can make it hard to accept test results that disagree with currently held beliefs.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How should information about defects and failures be communicated?
notes.back: In a constructive way.
notes.explanation: Some people regard testing as destructive even though it does much for project success and product quality; constructive reporting helps change that view.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester finds a serious defect in a feature the lead developer is proud of. Which way of reporting it fits the syllabus best?
notes.back: A: report it factually and constructively.
notes.choices:
A) Report it factually and constructively, focusing on the product and its users
B) Announce it at the team meeting as proof of careless work
C) Hold it back to avoid friction
notes.choicesExplained: B treats the report as criticism of the author, which is what testers must avoid. C withholds information stakeholders need.
notes.explanation: Test results can feel like criticism, so the syllabus asks for constructive communication.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.1 “Generic Skills Required for Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: From which practice does the whole team approach come?
notes.back: Extreme Programming.
notes.explanation: Extreme Programming is covered with other development practices in chapter 2 of the syllabus.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the whole team approach, who is responsible for quality?
notes.back: Everyone in the team.
notes.explanation: Any team member with the needed knowledge and skills can perform any task.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why do team members in the whole team approach share a workspace, physical or virtual?
notes.back: Co-location makes communication and interaction easier.
notes.explanation: The shared workspace can be physical or virtual.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which advantage of the whole team approach concerns how the team functions as a group?
notes.back: It improves team dynamics.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists three advantages; this is one of them.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which advantage of the whole team approach concerns how members talk and work together?
notes.back: It enhances communication and collaboration within the team.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists three advantages; this is one of them.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which advantage of the whole team approach lets the team draw on all its different skill sets for the project?
notes.back: It creates synergy.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists three advantages; this is one of them.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the whole team approach, how do testers work with business representatives?
notes.back: They help them create suitable acceptance tests.
notes.explanation: Testers work closely with others so the desired quality levels are reached.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the whole team approach, what do testers agree with developers?
notes.back: The test strategy and the approach to test automation.
notes.explanation: Working together on these helps the team reach the desired quality levels.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can testers do as a result of working closely with the rest of the team?
notes.back: Transfer testing knowledge to other members and influence how the product is developed.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names these as results of testers working closely with the team.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is the whole team approach always appropriate?
notes.back: No. In some contexts, such as safety-critical ones, a high level of test independence may be needed instead.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names safety-critical situations as an example.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A supplier of railway signalling software is choosing how to organise testing. Which consideration from the syllabus applies most?
notes.back: B: a high level of test independence may be needed.
notes.choices:
A) The whole team approach suits every context
B) A high level of test independence may be needed, so the whole team approach may not fit
C) Testing must be done only by the developers
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the syllabus says the approach may not always be appropriate. C gives no independence at all.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names safety-critical situations as ones where a high level of test independence may be needed.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When the only tester is ill, a developer with the right skills picks up her test tasks for the week. Which approach does this reflect?
notes.back: The whole team approach.
notes.explanation: In this approach tasks are not tied to job titles: whoever has the skills can pick them up.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team moves its tester, developers and analyst into one shared online workspace and notices problems now get sorted out in minutes. Which advantage is showing?
notes.back: Enhanced communication and collaboration within the team.
notes.explanation: Sharing a workspace eases interaction, which is one of the listed advantages.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.2 “Whole Team Approach”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does a degree of independence make a tester more effective at finding defects?
notes.back: The author’s and the tester’s cognitive biases differ.
notes.explanation: Independence works because the tester does not share the author’s cognitive biases.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does independence replace familiarity with the work product?
notes.back: No. Authors can, for example, find many defects in their own work efficiently.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says independence is not a replacement for familiarity.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What level of independence is testing by the work product’s own author?
notes.back: No independence.
notes.explanation: The syllabus grades independence by how far the tester is from the author: same person, same team, same organisation, or outside it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What level of independence is testing by the author’s peers from the same team?
notes.back: Some independence.
notes.explanation: The syllabus grades independence by how far the tester is from the author: same person, same team, same organisation, or outside it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What level of independence is testing by testers from outside the author’s team but within the organisation?
notes.back: High independence.
notes.explanation: The syllabus grades independence by how far the tester is from the author: same person, same team, same organisation, or outside it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What level of independence is testing by testers from outside the organisation?
notes.back: Very high independence.
notes.explanation: The syllabus grades independence by how far the tester is from the author: same person, same team, same organisation, or outside it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An outside consultancy tests a council’s new benefits portal. What level of independence is this?
notes.back: Very high independence.
notes.explanation: The testers come from outside the organisation that produced the work.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer asks a colleague from her own team to test her change before merging. What level of independence is this?
notes.back: Some independence.
notes.explanation: A peer from the same team is one step removed from the author.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For most projects, how is it usually best to carry out testing in terms of independence?
notes.back: With multiple levels of independence.
notes.explanation: The syllabus hedges this as usually best, for most projects.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On a smart-meter project, each developer checks her own code, a colleague checks each change, and an outside laboratory tests the finished meter. Is this in line with the syllabus?
notes.back: Yes. It uses several levels of independence, which is usually best for most projects.
notes.explanation: It runs from no independence, through some, to very high.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the main benefit of independence of testing?
notes.back: Independent testers tend to spot different kinds of failures and defects from the ones developers find.
notes.explanation: The syllabus puts this down to their different backgrounds, technical perspectives and biases.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 23
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can an independent tester do with the assumptions stakeholders made during specification and implementation?
notes.back: Verify, challenge or disprove them.
notes.explanation: It is the second benefit of independence the syllabus names.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 23
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can the isolation of independent testers from the development team lead to?
notes.back: A lack of collaboration, communication problems, or an adversarial relationship with the developers.
notes.explanation: Isolation from the development team is the first drawback the syllabus names.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 23
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What may developers lose when testing is done independently?
notes.back: A sense of responsibility for quality.
notes.explanation: It is one of the drawbacks of independence the syllabus names.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 23
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How may independent testers come to be seen around release time?
notes.back: As a bottleneck, or as the people to blame for delays in release.
notes.explanation: It is one of the drawbacks of independence the syllabus names.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 23
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After testing is moved to an outside supplier, developers start saying “the testers will catch it” and stop checking their own work. Is this a benefit or a drawback of independence?
notes.back: B: a drawback.
notes.choices:
A) A benefit: independent testers find different defects
B) A drawback: developers may lose their sense of responsibility for quality
C) Neither: it has nothing to do with independence
notes.choicesExplained: A is a real benefit, but not what this describes. C is wrong: the syllabus names exactly this drawback.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists developers losing a sense of responsibility for quality as a drawback.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 23
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An external tester asks why the address form assumes every customer has a postcode, when the firm also sells to countries that do not use them. Which benefit of independence is this?
notes.back: Challenging assumptions made during specification and implementation.
notes.explanation: An independent tester can verify, challenge or disprove stakeholders’ assumptions.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.5.3 “Independence of Testing”, p. 23
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
